The Outpost Island Mine was a gold and tungsten producer 94 kilometres southeast of  Yellowknife, Northwest Territories on an island of Great Slave Lake. Gold was discovered here in 1935 by prospectors, and some development was undertaken in 1936-1938. Tungsten ores became valuable during World War II, so the owners (Slave Lake Gold Mines Limited) investigated the tungsten possibilities of the mine. It produced small amounts of gold, copper, and tungsten during 1941-1942, and then again in 1951-1952 during the Korean War. It was a small deposit and was not considered economic because of unpredictable tungsten market prices in the 1950s.

The Discovery Mine was a gold mine 81 kilometers northeast (approx bearing of 15 degrees) of Yellowknife, Northwest Territories that operated between 1950 and 1969. Gold was discovered here by Alfred Giauque in 1944. A complete townsite, on Giauque Lake, was established by the company to house workers and their families. The mine produced one million troy ounces (31,000 kg) of gold from one million tons of ore. The abandoned townsite, not accessible by road, was demolished in 2005.

This table provides a detailed overview of various fruits along with their scientific names, companion plants that help them grow, plants that they are helped by, plants that attract beneficial organisms, and those that repel or distract pests. 

Starting with apples, scientifically known as Malus domestica, they benefit from the presence of clover, chives, garlic, leeks, nasturtium, southernwood, daffodils, and comfrey. However, apples are sensitive to cedar trees due to the apple-cedar rust and should be planted away from walnut trees, as the roots of walnuts produce growth inhibitors that can adversely affect apple trees.

Next, apricots, or Prunus armeniaca, do not have any specific beneficial companions listed but should be avoided near peppers. This is because a fungus that affects peppers can also harm apricot trees significantly.

Blueberries, classified under Vaccinium spp., thrive in the company of oak trees, pine trees, strawberries, clover, bay laurel, dewberries, and yarrow. The acidic soil created by pine and oak trees is essential for blueberries, while strawberries and dewberries provide healthy ground cover. Clover is particularly beneficial as it fixes nitrogen, which blueberries require in high amounts. Additionally, yarrow and bay laurel help repel harmful insects, and all the listed companions prefer the acidic soil that blueberries need.

The category of fruit trees, encompassing various species, benefits from the presence of alliums, tansy, nasturtiums, marigolds, marjoram, lemon balm, mustards, dandelions, and borage. However, no specific plants to avoid are mentioned for this category.

Grapes, belonging to the genus 'Vitis', are supported by companions such as hyssop, alyssum, basil, beans, chives, geraniums, mustards, oregano, clover, peas, and blackberries. There are no specific plants that help repel pests for grapes, but it is advised to keep them away from cabbage, garlic, and radishes.

Melons, identified as Cucumis melo, benefit from the presence of chamomile, pigweed, summer savoury, and sow thistle, although there are no specific plants to avoid listed for melons.

Passion fruit, scientifically known as Passiflora edulis, is supported by a variety of plants including potatoes, beets, Swiss chard, carrots, spinach, strawberries, eggplants, onions, leeks, and lettuce. However, it is recommended to avoid planting passion fruit near cucurbits, maize, cowpea, sorghum, okra, and sweet potatoes.

Pears, classified under Pyrus spp., are noted to benefit from aromatic plants, although no specific companions or plants to avoid are mentioned.

Finally, strawberries, known as Fragaria × ananassa, thrive alongside bush beans, lettuce, onions, spinach, and passion fruit. They are helped by caraway, bush beans, lupin, onions, sage, thyme, and borage.
